name: PT Estika Tata Tiara Tbk

frontmatter.title: Estika Tata Tiara — a licensed meat importer priced as a growth franchise
frontmatter.summary: We initiate Estika Tata Tiara at SELL with a target of Rp58, -84.3% from the last price. A thin-spread beef importer whose private import allocation was cut to a small slice of the national quota, it does not generate free cash, funds inventory with bank debt and trades above the ceiling its board set for its own buyback. The target is a trailing-multiple ceiling: on our own forward earnings the shares are worth less.
thesis: A trading licence, not a brand. Almost all revenue is imported-meat distribution at a gross margin in the mid single digits, and Food Processing is a rounding error against group sales [S2].

The quota is the moat, and the private slice of it has been cut sharply. The private import allocation fell to 30,000 t for 2026 from 180,000 t, a small fraction of a 297,000 t national quota, so state traders now hold the import channel that sheltered private distributors [S5, S9].
The balance sheet, not the P&L, is the story. Inventory growth and the withdrawal of supplier credit turned operating cash flow negative in FY2024, and net debt now sits at 6.1x EBITDA [S2].
The market pays a growth multiple for a business whose cash flow cannot service its debt on the company's own capex plan; the board's buyback ceiling sits below the traded price [S3].
Dairy is real optionality but not yet revenue — the herd and the Sukabumi land enter the valuation at their sourced biological-asset carrying value, not through hope [S2, S4].

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of Estika Tata Tiara at SELL with a target of Rp58, a return of -84.3% from the last price of Rp372. The shares trade on a market capitalisation of IDR3,020.7bn after a twelve-month range of Rp127 to Rp780 [S0]. Our view is not that the company is a fraud or that the beef business is disappearing. It is that the market is paying a growth multiple for a licensed trading spread that is being withdrawn, while the balance sheet that funds it has become the binding constraint.

Estika is not the branded meat processor its name suggests. The Distribution and Sales segment contributed IDR6,471.4bn of IDR6,474.3bn of FY2025 revenue; Food Processing, home of the Kibif and Boss brands, contributed IDR13.5bn [S2 p.15]. The group earns a gross margin of 6.3% and a net margin of 2.0%, which is what a quota-protected importer earns, not what a consumer franchise earns [S2]. The profit is real: net profit reached IDR129.1bn in FY2025. But it is the return on a licence, and the licence is the thing that changed.

Our variant view turns on the import regime. For 2026 the private-sector beef import allocation was cut to 30,000 t from 180,000 t, leaving private importers a small slice of a national quota of 297,000 t, so the state did not shrink the import channel, it reallocated it [S9, S5]. Two independent associations, APPDI and Nampa, give the same private figures, and the state traders Berdikari and PPI were allocated 100,000 t of what remains [S9, S5]. The national deficit is not the problem — BEEF itself discloses a raw-material gap of 271,818 t [S2 p.41]. The problem is who is allowed to fill it. The company does not disclose its own 2026 permit tonnage; its last quota disclosure is the 2018–20 allocation of 12,000 head of live cattle, which is a measure of how far the licence has moved since [S2 p.63]. A distributor whose access to the raw material is rationed by the state, and increasingly rationed in favour of state competitors, cannot compound the way its history suggests.

The financial signature is already visible. FY2025 operating cash flow was IDR-124.9bn against net profit of IDR129.1bn, because inventory rose to IDR907.6bn while payables to the controlling group were cut to IDR4.7bn from IDR378.6bn and advances to suppliers collapsed [S2]. That was not the first year of the burn: FY2024 operating cash flow was IDR-703.9bn, so FY2025 is a fraction of the prior year's outflow rather than the onset of it, and the two-year record is still cash consumed in both years [S2 p.263]. Capex of IDR507.0bn was funded with bank debt, leaving net debt of IDR1,545.6bn, or 6.1x EBITDA [S0, S2]. In our base case the revenue base shrinks to IDR4,752.1bn in FY2026E and net profit falls to IDR33.8bn. Free cash flow to the firm is positive in FY2026E (IDR247.6bn) because a falling revenue base releases working capital, and turns negative again in FY2027E (IDR-58.4bn) as the book is rebuilt and capex runs ahead of depreciation; net debt therefore falls to IDR1,388.1bn, or 7.5x EBITDA, and then rises in every later year to IDR1,955.8bn by FY2035E [S0]. This is not a cautious forecast: it is the last actual's margin re-priced at the current cost of debt, with revenue at the filed first-half run-rate and every cash-flow gap funded with bank lines that pay interest.

The target is a blend of three lenses, and the blend arithmetic matters. The P/E leg values the business at Rp153 on 9.6x peer-median earnings, the EV/EBITDA leg at Rp61 on 7.1x, and the DCF leg at Rp0 because its equity value is negative before the floor [S0]. The blend of Rp52 therefore sits below the EV/EBITDA leg, not above it, and 60.0% of the weight is a floored zero: the target is carried by the P/E leg diluted by a smaller EV leg. At Rp372 the market is paying 89.4x forward earnings and 23.8x forward EV/EBITDA for that stream [S0]. The board's buyback authorisation carries a maximum price of Rp300 per share — below the last traded price — which is a statement of what the company was willing to pay for its own shares, not an estimate of their value [S3].

Three things move the value: the 2027 allocation, capex discipline in the dairy build, and the normalisation of working capital. We treat each in the valuation and risk sections. The bear case is a debt spiral; the bull case is a state-backed offtake contract that turns the cold chain into a fee business. Neither is our base case, and the scenarios are mirrored except for the credit spread, which can widen but cannot fall. The published target is the base case, not a probability-weighted blend: the engine's multiple legs read trailing market data and its DCF is floored in every case, so weighting the three cases would manufacture a precision the model does not have [S0].

Estika Tata Tiara began as a beef importer and butcher's shop, listed in 2019, and then spent its first two years as a public company in a debt restructuring. The annual report's milestone table records the insolvency petition, the debt settlement agreement, and the debt-to-equity swap that made Asia Agri International the controlling shareholder, followed by a change of management [S2 p.63]. That history matters for the business model: the company was rebuilt around licensed import access and a cold chain, not around a consumer brand. In June 2024 it acquired three distributors — Fajar Jaya Anugerah, Sinar Wijaya Utama and Sukses International Anugerah Pratama — in what the annual report itself classifies as material and affiliated transactions, and those entities are now the revenue base [S2 p.124, p.266].

The group describes six business lines: a feedlot at Subang with capacity for 6,000 head, a ruminant slaughterhouse at the same site, a cold-store complex with 22,000 pallets and a 28,000 t store commissioned in November 2025, imported-meat distribution, processed-meat manufacturing under the Kibif, Boss, Adell, Murato and Kipao brands, and a dairy farm and milk plant under development [S2 p.23, p.62; S7]. The factories are at Cikarang and Subang in West Java and Salatiga in Central Java; the dairy herd is at Banyumas and the new dairy land is at Sukabumi [S2 p.62; S4]. The company employed 825 people at the last count [S0].

The revenue mix is the single most important fact about this company. Distribution and Sales produced IDR6,471.4bn of the IDR6,474.3bn group total in FY2025; Food Processing produced IDR13.5bn [S2 p.15]. The branded business that the company markets at trade fairs and in its annual report is therefore a calling card, not the earnings engine. What the group actually does is buy, import, store and distribute beef and cattle, earning a spread between the landed cost and the domestic wholesale price. Its customers are supermarkets, hotels, restaurants and catering operators, and food processors, with a smaller direct-to-consumer channel through marketplaces [S2 p.40, p.41; S7]. Kibif products are sold on all five major islands, according to the milestone table [S2 p.63].

Market position is best described as a licensed challenger. The company says it has secured a share of the processed-meat market among the large fast-moving consumer goods producers, but it does not disclose a percentage, and its own segment accounts show that the branded business is tiny relative to distribution [S2 p.40, p.15]. In imported beef it is one of a small set of quota holders, competing with state traders and other private importers; the quota allocation is the relevant measure of position, not brand share [S5]. The strategic direction is vertical integration — feedlot, abattoir, cold storage, processing, distribution and now dairy — which raises the capital intensity of what is economically a trading business [S2 p.62; S4].

Ownership is concentrated. Asia Agri International holds 70.6% of the shares, individual shareholder Edie holds 8.1%, and the public holds 21.3% as of 31 December 2025 [S2 p.81]. The controlling block came from the debt restructuring, so the controller is also the group's historical lender and supplier — a relationship we return to in the governance section. The board disclosed in the annual report comprises three commissioners, one of them independent, and a president director; press in November 2026 attributes the president-director role to Ari Wijayanto, which we read as a change during the year that we have not yet seen in a filing [S2 p.32, p.48; S4]. For a company whose value depends on a government licence, the relationship between the controller, the board and the quota allocation is a governance question, not a footnote.

Indonesia does not produce enough beef. The annual report puts national demand for beef and buffalo meat at 787,415 t and domestic production at 515,597 t, a raw-material deficit of 271,818 t [S2 p.41]. The deficit is structural rather than cyclical: demand is pulled by population, urbanisation, the hotel-restaurant-catering channel and the processed-food industry, while domestic herd productivity is constrained by smallholder ownership, feed costs and land [S2 p.41]. The government's answer has been to manage the gap through import quotas for live cattle and frozen beef, not through an open licence [S2 p.63]. That makes the quota the central economic variable for every private processor and importer, and it makes policy the industry's main risk.

The quota regime tightened sharply for private importers in 2026. The processors' associations APPDI and Nampa both put the private-sector allocation at 30,000 t for 2026 against 180,000 t the year before, and both place it inside a national quota of 297,000 t [S9, S5]. The early reading of this file — that the national quota itself had been cut to the private figure — was wrong, and the correction matters in the opposite direction from what one might expect: the state did not reduce the import channel, it took it. State traders Berdikari and PPI were allocated at least 100,000 t, and Nampa reports that private processors and association members were left with 17,000 t of the private slice [S5]. The itemised allocations do not sum to the 297,000 t total, so we treat the split as directional evidence of concentration rather than a reconciled schedule, and we found no published Kepmentan or Bapanas schedule in the archived sources; the association arithmetic is the best available, and it is corroborated by two independent associations. What is not in doubt is the direction: private importers are being pushed toward domestic cattle and whatever quota they can still obtain. The association warns of idle processing capacity and of import permits whose approved meat cuts do not match customer demand [S5], and a separate policy track — the cattle-oil-palm integration programme SISKA — is designed to displace about a third of beef imports over time, which is a volume risk that does not depend on the annual quota at all [S9].

Prices reflect the squeeze. By February 2026 fresh beef was trading at the top of the government's reference-price band, and buffalo meat was above its reference price, after a supply disruption [S5]. For a distributor with a thin gross margin, a raw-material price at the administrative ceiling and a quota that is allocated rather than auctioned is a margin problem that cannot be solved by branding. It also explains why BEEF's own gross margin is a spread on a regulated input, not a pricing decision.

The dairy opportunity is the mirror image: a structural deficit with a policy tailwind. The company cites Ministry of Agriculture data showing national milk requirement of 4.68 m t against domestic production of 820,900 t and imports of 3.86 m t, i.e. most of the market is imported [S4]. Demand policy is a possible pull, but none of it is contracted to BEEF and no filing quantifies the dairy's revenue or its start date [S4, S2]. The economics are attractive in principle — fresh milk, pasteurisation and eventually UHT — but BEEF's starting point is 250 imported cows and 30.05 ha of Sukabumi land, a sub-scale position against incumbent dairies and importers [S4]. We treat dairy as a real option funded by capex, not as a business with a defensible share today.

Competition in beef distribution is fragmented at the customer end and concentrated at the licence end. State traders Berdikari and PPI now hold the largest import allocations [S5]; private importers, feedlots and processors compete for the remainder; modern retail and HORECA buyers run tenders and have alternatives in chicken, fish and eggs. BEEF's advantages are its cold-chain density — the Subang store and pallet capacity, the Cikarang and Salatiga plants, the Subang feedlot and abattoir — and its halal and food-safety certifications, which are prerequisites rather than differentiators [S2 p.21, p.23, p.62]. Its disadvantage is that the licence, which is the real barrier to entry, is being reallocated away from it.

On the five forces: supplier power is high and rising, because the quota holder sets the terms; buyer power is moderate to high, because retail and HORECA are concentrated and the product is undifferentiated; rivalry is high, because beef distribution is a commodity spread with many licensed and unlicensed participants; substitutes are strong, because poultry, fish and eggs are cheaper proteins; and barriers to entry are regulatory and capital-intensive but not technological, so a well-connected entrant with a quota can appear quickly [S2 p.41; S5]. The moat, such as it is, is a licence plus a cold chain — and half of that moat is a policy choice that has already been reversed once.

The external drivers we model are the feed complex and the rupiah. Corn and soymeal are the feed inputs behind domestic cattle prices; our agri deck has corn at US$214.6 and soymeal at US$411.0 for FY2026E, both above spot and well above their FY2025 averages, and we hold the FY2025A gross margin at base input costs so that the deck's cost path, with four-fifths of it passed through, lands FY2026E on the audited margin rather than below it [S0]. Because the selling price sits inside a government reference band that is revised when costs move, we assume four-fifths of a feed-cost move is passed on with a lag rather than half; the filed first-half 2026 gross profit is above the FY2025 rate and its EBIT margin is in line with it, which is the calibration the earlier half-pass-through assumption failed [S0, S5]. Imported beef is dollar-priced, and the rupiah is forecast at 18,350 by FY2027E on the house macro deck, so a weaker currency raises the landed cost of the raw material that the quota already rations [S0]. Energy costs for cold storage and cold-chain logistics are the third external input, and the annual report names them as a primary cost pressure [S2 p.41]. None of these is within management's control; all of them pass through a gross margin of 6.3%.

The reported history is a series of step changes, not a growth curve. Revenue went from IDR39.1bn in FY2022A to IDR611.8bn in FY2023A, IDR4,930.8bn in FY2024A and IDR6,474.3bn in FY2025A; net profit went from IDR-93.6bn to IDR57.1bn to IDR103.0bn to IDR129.3bn over the same years [S0]. The FY2024 step is the consolidation of the three acquired distributors, and the FY2025 step is the full year of their revenue plus the import spike in the first quarter [S2 p.124; S0]. A reader should not extrapolate the revenue CAGR: the base year was a restructured shell, and the growth came from acquisition and import volume, not from like-for-like demand.

FY2025 is the cleanest picture of the economics. Revenue of IDR6,474.3bn produced gross profit of IDR410.9bn, a gross margin of 6.3%; operating expenses of IDR188.9bn left EBIT of IDR222.1bn and EBITDA of IDR254.1bn; interest of IDR65.6bn and IDR4.4bn of other income took pre-tax profit to IDR160.9bn, and tax of IDR31.8bn left net profit of IDR129.1bn [S0]. The margins tell the story: EBITDA margin of 3.9% and net margin of 2.0% [S0]. The reported return on equity of 39.7% is flattered by a thin equity base after the restructuring, not by high returns on capital; the balance sheet carries debt of IDR1,564.1bn against equity of IDR390.1bn [S0].

The FY2025 cash-flow statement is the most important document in this file. Operating cash flow was IDR-124.9bn while net profit was IDR129.1bn, a gap wider than the whole of net profit. The cause is working capital: inventory rose from IDR277.3bn to IDR907.6bn, an increase of 227.0%, while trade payables to the controlling group fell from IDR378.6bn to IDR4.7bn and advances to suppliers fell from IDR841.5bn to IDR26.0bn [S2 p.258-259]. In other words, the supplier-funded inventory model that had financed the business was replaced with bank debt and the company's own cash. The two-year record puts that in context: FY2024 operating cash flow was IDR-703.9bn, so FY2025's IDR-124.9bn is a much smaller outflow, not a new one — the burn was cut sharply, and a reader who takes FY2025 alone as the deterioration has the trend backwards [S2 p.263]. Capex of IDR507.0bn, or 7.8% of revenue, was the Subang cold store and the distributor integration [S2 p.23]. Free cash flow to the firm was IDR-883.9bn [S0]. Net debt ended the year at IDR1,545.6bn, 6.1x EBITDA, with short-term bank loans of IDR1,132.4bn and cash of IDR18.5bn [S0, S2].

Our forecast anchors on the last actual and the company's own disclosures. FY2026E revenue is IDR4,752.1bn, revenue growth of -26.6% on FY2025: the first half of 2026 annualises to the base we use, and the second quarter was barely ahead of the prior year, so the decline is the absence of the 2025 import spike rather than a collapse in the customer base; we assume no second-half recovery because no order book, quota restoration or seasonality supports one [S0]. Gross margin holds at 6.3%, essentially the FY2025A rate: our agri deck has corn and soymeal above base-year levels and four-fifths of that is passed through, and we anchor the constant-price input on the audited FY2025 margin so the deck's cost path lands on the last actual rather than drifting below it [S0]. EBITDA is IDR185.0bn, interest rises to IDR115.7bn as the higher debt is repriced, and net profit falls to IDR33.8bn [S0]. Working capital releases cash in FY2026E because revenue falls faster than the balance sheet can adjust, which is why free cash flow to the firm is IDR247.6bn in the first year and turns negative again in FY2027E (IDR-58.4bn) as the working-capital book is rebuilt on a growing revenue base [S0]. From FY2027E we hold revenue at the filed quarterly run-rate and let it converge on the long-run nominal GDP rate, with capex stepping down from the dairy build to maintenance-plus-growth; net profit moves to IDR45.3bn and to IDR41.9bn by FY2030E [S0]. Even on that recovery, the model does not produce a sustained positive free-cash-flow year in the forecast horizon beyond the first-year working-capital release: capex plus working capital absorbs EBITDA, the funding gap is carried as new bank lines every year, and net debt rises to IDR1,955.8bn by FY2035E, or 8.3x EBITDA, with interest of IDR141.5bn [S0]. The financing line is not an appetite assumption: each year's net borrowing is the pre-financing deficit, so cash is held at about the June 2026 balance of IDR18.5bn and the gap is interest-bearing debt, not idle cash earning a yield below the cost of the debt that funds it [S0]. That is the single most important output of this model, and it is why the rating is not simply a multiple-based call.

The earnings-quality screen is optics-class, not manipulation-class, but it is a flag and not a pass. The accruals test is net profit less operating cash flow, over average total assets. In FY2025A net profit of IDR129.1bn against operating cash flow of IDR-124.9bn is a gap wider than the whole of net profit, equal to about eleven per cent of average total assets — which were IDR2,195.0bn at end-FY2024A and IDR2,364.6bn at end-FY2025A [S2 p.258, S0]. That is above the house screen's ten per cent line, not under it. FY2024A was far worse: the same arithmetic on a much smaller asset base gives nearly fifty-six per cent, so the screen flags two consecutive years of earnings outrunning cash, not one [S0]. What it also shows is a one-year improvement rather than a persistent trend: FY2023A generated positive operating cash flow, and the FY2025A gap is a fraction of the FY2024A one [S0]. The reason we classify it as optics rather than manipulation is that the gap is a disclosed, physical working-capital build, not a revenue-recognition artefact: inventory rose from IDR277.3bn to IDR907.6bn, payables to the controlling group were cut from IDR378.6bn to IDR4.7bn and advances to suppliers fell from IDR841.5bn to IDR26.0bn [S2 p.258-259]. Trade receivables of IDR217.8bn grew 57.3% against revenue growth of 31.3%, which is a divergence flag under the house screen [S2 p.99]. Optics-class carries a haircut rather than a pass, and ours is in the forecast: the working-capital ratio is the FY2025A one, so the inflated inventory balance is assumed to persist and consume cash in every forecast year instead of being normalised back to the FY2024A level. A manipulation-class finding would kill the name, and there is none here. On the special-monitoring-board and notation screens the name is clean; the flag that does apply is structure, not fabrication [S2 p.32].

Capital allocation is where the governance and the numbers meet. The company pays no dividend — it distributed nothing for FY2025 [S2 p.115] — while it committed up to IDR100.0bn to a buyback at a maximum price of Rp300 per share, funded, the announcement says, from internal cash [S3]. The shares now trade above that ceiling, so any repurchase at the authorised price is executed below the market; even so, it consumes cash that a balance sheet with negative free cash flow needs. Capex is the other call: a distributor with a gross margin of 6.3% spent IDR507.0bn on cold storage in FY2025 and plans to spend IDR237.6bn in FY2026E on dairy and land [S0, S2]. Until the dairy produces revenue, that is growth capex with no visible return, and it is the reason the DCF is negative.

We flag two structure items explicitly. First, the June 2024 acquisitions were affiliated transactions, and the previous shareholders of the acquired distributors are disclosed as related parties, including a member of the board [S2 p.124, p.306]. Second, the auditor disclosure does not reconcile. The shareholders' resolution in the report names KAP Independen Drs Kartoyo dan Rekan (translated as Kartoyo and Partners) as the firm that audited the FY2025 statements [S2 p.136-137], but the governance table on the same report lists Heliantono dan Rekan for FY2025, Urda Zismawan for FY2024 and Irfan Zulmendra for FY2023 [S2 p.180], and Heliantono dan Rekan also appears in the service-fee table [S2 p.87]. We cannot establish from the archived text which firm signed the FY2025 opinion or whether the firm changed at all; what we can say is that the report names a different firm or engagement partner in each of its three disclosed years and does not explain the rotation. That is a disclosure flag, not a conclusion about audit quality, and we have not treated it as evidence of wrongdoing.

We value Estika on a blended DCF, P/E and EV/EBITDA set because the company is a levered, asset-backed distributor of a commodity, not a branded compounder. The DCF is the primary method because the balance sheet — not the trading margin — determines whether equity has value: with debt of IDR1,564.1bn and equity of IDR390.1bn, a small change in the operating cash flow accrues almost entirely to or from the shareholders. P/E and EV/EBITDA are the cross-checks the market uses for an IDX consumer name, and they also test whether the DCF's negative answer is an artefact of our capex assumptions [S0].

The cost of capital is built from a risk-free rate of 7.4%, a mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2%, a country risk premium of 2.5%, and a levered beta of 0.96 derived from the food-sector unlevered beta and the company's debt-to-equity ratio of 0.47. The two premiums are added and multiplied by the beta, and the Indonesian default spread of 1.6% is then deducted because it is already embedded in the rupiah risk-free rate; that gives a cost of equity of 12.2%. Debt is 32.1% of capital at a pre-tax cost of 9.4%, and the weighted average cost of capital is 10.7%. The cost of equity sits inside the house compounder band for IDR names, which runs from eleven to thirteen per cent; the WACC is below that band only because rupiah debt is a third of the capital structure, and we do not lift it into the band to manufacture discipline. The DCF is already floored at zero, so a higher discount rate makes the equity more negative rather than more defensible, and the band the house card sets is a cost-of-equity band, which this build satisfies. Two cost-of-debt rates appear in this file and they measure different things: the WACC charges 9.4%, the market rate on new corporate rupiah debt, while the P&L forecast charges 7.4% on opening debt, the rate the filed first-half 2026 interest bill implies on the average balance, a higher figure than the FY2025 average because the debt stepped up through 2025 [S2 p.261, S0]. The below-band WACC is not the flattering choice it looks: the terminal value carries most of the enterprise value, so a higher discount rate lowers it and makes the equity more negative, which is why the DCF is a solvency test rather than a sensitive price [S0].

The DCF produces a negative equity value — enterprise value of IDR588.4bn against net debt of the 30 June 2026 balance sheet (bank debt less cash, the figure the engine's bridge takes, not the FY2025A year-end IDR1,545.6bn) — which the engine floors at Rp0 rather than publishing a negative share price; it carries 60.0% of the target weight [S0]. The mechanism is simple: EBITDA of IDR185.0bn in FY2026E is taxed, and then capex of IDR237.6bn and a working-capital balance above one trillion rupiah absorb the operating cash flow; in the terminal year free cash flow to the firm of roughly IDR48.4bn against a 10.7% cost of capital and 4.0% growth is not enough to cover a debt stack that has grown to IDR1,955.8bn. We are explicit about what that means: the DCF is a solvency signal, not a price target in the ordinary sense. It says that on the company's own capex and working-capital plan the equity is worth nothing unless something changes — a capex cut, a margin recovery, an equity injection or an asset sale.

The cross-checks disagree, and the disagreement is the point. The P/E leg values the shares at Rp153, applying the food-sector peer median of 9.6x to FY2025 parent earnings of IDR129.3bn; the EV/EBITDA leg values them at Rp61, applying the peer median of 7.1x to EBITDA of IDR254.1bn, then deducting the same 30 June 2026 net debt, adding the IDR110.8bn dairy carrying value and the associate investment balance and deducting the minority interest — the bridge that produces that share price. Both legs are peer-median only: we have removed BEEF's own trading history from the multiple, because the own-history mean rests on three observations over a period in which the company was a restructured shell and then an acquisition story, and blending it into the target was letting a Rp372 share price partly value itself. The P/E leg ignores the capital structure; the EV/EBITDA leg does not. For a company whose equity is a thin layer over debt, the EV-based answer is the more credible one, and it is the lower of the two. Both legs also share a generous earnings base: they capitalise the last actual year, whose net profit the base case cuts to IDR33.8bn and whose EBITDA the base case cuts to IDR185.0bn.

Apply the two legs to the base case's own earnings and the target's support becomes explicit. The same 9.6x peer median on FY2026E earnings per share of 4.16 gives a base-case-consistent value of roughly seven-tenths of the published target, and the EV/EBITDA leg floors at zero on forward numbers because FY2026E EBITDA of IDR185.0bn against net debt of IDR1,388.1bn does not cover a 7.1x multiple. So the published target is a trailing-multiple ceiling, not a base-case-consistent value: it is generous against forward earnings and cheap against the trailing earnings the legs actually use. A reader who believes our forecast should value the shares near the forward P/E leg, not at the target [S0].

The blended value is Rp52; the published target of Rp58 rolls that value forward one year at the cost of equity, a convention the engine applies uniformly. The weights are 60.0% DCF, 30.0% P/E and 10.0% EV/EBITDA, the industry template. We did not drop the DCF to make the target look less extreme: a valuation that ignored the cash-flow statement would be the wrong answer for this balance sheet. Equally, we did not let the floored DCF set the published target on its own, because a zero is not a price. What the arithmetic means, plainly, is three things a reader should hold onto. First, 60.0% of the weight is a floored zero, so the DCF contributes nothing to the published number even though it is the method we trust most for this balance sheet. Second, the blend of Rp52 is below the EV/EBITDA leg of Rp61, not above it: the P/E leg at Rp153 is what carries the target, diluted by the smaller EV/EBITDA leg. Third, at the target the shares would trade on trailing earnings per share of 15.92 and forward earnings per share of 4.16: cheap against the 9.6x peer median on the trailing figure, and well above it on the forward figure the base case actually produces. The target is therefore generous against forward earnings and cheap against trailing earnings, which is what a trailing-multiple ceiling is. That is a de-rating call, not a liquidation call, and the reader can see exactly how thin the support underneath it is [S0].

The two assumptions that carry most of the value are the gross margin and the capex rate; revenue growth matters less because the margin is thin and the working-capital release from a smaller revenue base partly offsets it. A percentage point on gross margin is worth several times a percentage point on revenue growth, and a capex rate held at the FY2025 level rather than stepped down would make the DCF negative even in the terminal year. The sensitivity table shows the grid; the direction is unambiguous [S0]. The third input is the cost of debt, because interest of IDR115.7bn is charged on opening debt before any dividend or growth spend [S0]. Working capital is not on the grid, so we disclose it here: the terminal year absorbs IDR45.5bn of working capital at the ratio we set, and the earlier draft's annualised ratio — the June balance over half-year revenue doubled — added roughly a third again to that drag, which is what turned the terminal value negative. The ratio we now use is the FY2025-revenue ratio, and it keeps the model internally consistent with the revenue base [S2, S0].

What does the price imply? At Rp372 the shares trade at 89.4x our FY2026E earnings, 23.8x FY2026E EV/EBITDA and 7.1x book [S0]. The reverse DCF does not solve: the price is not bracketed by any revenue-growth assumption we would defend, which is another way of saying that the market is not valuing the current business on its cash flows at all. The multiple-survival test fails too. A rational buyer of a beef distributor with a gross margin of 6.3% would not pay 23.8x EBITDA for it, and the company itself set a buyback ceiling of Rp300 per share, an authorisation rather than a valuation; the market trades above that ceiling [S3]. The dominant IDX quality de-rating of the past decade is the relevant base rate: premium multiples on structurally challenged consumer names have not survived. Our target is a de-rating to a level the cash flows can support, not a forecast of business failure.
The risks that matter here are not the usual consumer-demand risks; they are licence, liquidity and governance risks that compound each other.

**Regulatory and quota (likelihood high, impact high).** The 2026 allocation cut the private processors' share to 17,000 t and concentrated the import channel in state traders [S5]. A further cut, or an allocation that leaves BEEF without commercially usable permits, removes the raw material for the distribution business. The association's complaint that permits do not match the meat cuts customers want shows that even an allocated quota can be economically unusable [S5]. This is the largest single risk and it is not diversifiable within the company.

**Liquidity and refinancing (likelihood medium to high, impact high).** FY2025 operating cash flow was IDR-124.9bn after IDR-703.9bn in FY2024, net debt was IDR1,545.6bn or 6.1x EBITDA, most of the debt is short-term, and cash was IDR18.5bn [S0, S2]. On our forecast, net debt rises to IDR1,955.8bn and the company funds a cash-flow gap with new bank lines every year, so interest is charged on the debt the gap creates rather than on a frozen balance. A bank that declines to roll a facility, or prices it wider, forces an equity raise or an asset sale; a rights issue would have to be struck at a discount to a share price already unable to cover the debt, so it transfers value to the new money rather than creating any. The interest bill of IDR115.7bn is already charged before maintenance capex.

**Liquidity of the shares (impact medium).** The public float is 11.7% with the controller at 70.6%, and three-month average daily turnover is IDR2.7bn, a thin fraction of the market capitalisation [S0, S2 p.81]. The house liquidity schedule applies no discount at that turnover, so none is applied; but a holder who needs to exit a position of any size is dependent on the controller's stake staying still, and the buyback authorisation is the only bid the company itself has committed to [S3].

**Margin and commodity (likelihood high, impact medium).** Gross margin is 6.3%; our agri deck has corn and soymeal above spot for FY2026E, and we assume 80.0% of the feed-cost increase passes through, the unpassed fifth being the lag before the reference-price band is revised rather than a standing squeeze [S0]. Fresh beef was already at the top of the government's reference-price band in early 2026, which limits the ability to pass cost on [S5]. A one-point margin miss on revenue of IDR4,752.1bn is larger than the entire FY2026E net profit.

**Currency (likelihood medium, impact medium).** Imported beef and dairy equipment are dollar-priced; the house macro deck has the rupiah at 18,350 per dollar by FY2027E, and a weaker currency raises the landed cost of the very input the quota rations [S0]. The company does not disclose a hedging policy in the annual report, so we assume the exposure is unhedged [S2].

**Operational and food safety (likelihood low to medium, impact high).** Production is concentrated in a small number of plants and one abattoir; a food-safety incident, a disease outbreak or a cold-chain failure would hit both the branded business and the licence to operate. The company holds halal and food-safety certifications, which are the minimum for the trade rather than a protection against failure [S2 p.21].

**Governance and related parties (likelihood medium, impact medium).** The controller holds 70.6% of the shares; the group was the working-capital lender before the banks; long-term other payables to related parties were IDR194.8bn at end-2025; and the 2024 acquisitions were affiliated transactions [S2 p.259, p.124]. The buyback at a ceiling of Rp300 per share while the shares trade higher is a capital-allocation choice made by the same controller [S3]. We do not allege diversion; we do say that minority shareholders have limited ability to influence the allocation of cash between the listed company and its controlling group.

**Execution of the dairy build (likelihood medium, impact medium).** The dairy business rests on 250 imported cows and 30.05 ha of land, with a milk factory still to be built [S4]. Capital needs are front-loaded and revenue is back-loaded; a delay or overrun consumes the free cash flow the beef business does not have. We do not carry the dairy at zero: the herd and the Sukabumi land enter the valuation at the IDR110.8bn biological-asset carrying value, the only sourced anchor available while the land consideration and the milk-plant budget remain undisclosed [S2, S4]. That value is small against the market capitalisation and it does not pay interest. The domestic milk deficit is real (4.68 m t of demand against 820,900 t of production) but the incumbents and importers already serve it [S4].

The three cases shock the same drivers in opposite directions, so the scenario set is mirrored except for the credit spread, which can widen in the bear and cannot fall in the bull below the BI rate already in the input. In the base case, revenue growth is -26.6% in FY2026E, gross margin is 6.3%, capex steps down from the dairy peak, and net debt falls to IDR1,388.1bn; the target is Rp58. In the bear case, revenue growth and gross margin are lowered by the mirrored amounts: the private allocation is cut again in 2027, the trading spread compresses, and the model's negative free cash flow requires a refinancing at a wider spread or an equity injection. In the bull case, the same two drivers move up by the same amounts: the 2027 allocation is restored toward the 2025 level, the school-meal programme gives the cold chain a visible offtake, the Subang store runs at higher throughput without new capex, and the margin holds. We do not publish a probability-weighted target. The engine's multiple legs read trailing market data and its DCF is floored at zero in the base and bear cases, so all three cases come out at the same published number; a weighted average would therefore be the base case dressed as a distribution [S0].

One mechanical point a reader should know: because the DCF's equity value is negative in the base and bear cases, and because the P/E and EV/EBITDA legs are anchored on trailing market data rather than on the forecast, the three cases do not produce three different published targets. The differentiation is in the forecast lines and in the conditions below, not in the target arithmetic, and that is why the number we publish is labelled a base-case target and not a blend [S0]. The bear's operating case is worse than the base by design — revenue growth and margin lower by the mirrored shocks, and a refinancing cost that the base does not carry — and if the bear operating path is realised the equity is worth less than our target, not the same. We would rather say that plainly than publish a weighted number that implies the distribution has a centre.

The signposts that would change our view are specific. A 2027 quota that restores the private processors' share, or a multi-year offtake contract under the school-meal programme, would move us toward the bull case. A gross margin sustained above the FY2025 level for two quarters, with operating cash flow turning positive, would tell us the working-capital build has normalised. A capex cut to maintenance, or a decision to slow the dairy build until it has an offtake contract, would improve the DCF materially. On the other side, a failed rollover of the short-term bank lines, a further quota cut, or a related-party receivable or guarantee that we have not seen would move us toward the bear case. We would review the rating on any of these before the next scheduled refresh.

Ownership is the first fact of governance here. Asia Agri International holds 70.6% of the shares, individual shareholder Edie holds 8.1%, and the public holds 21.3% [S2 p.81]. The free float implied by the market data is 11.7%, with insiders at 80.7%, so the shares are thin and the controller can set the agenda [S0]. The block came from the debt-to-equity swap that resolved the insolvency, which means the controller is not a financial sponsor with an exit clock; it is the group's historical creditor and counterparty [S2 p.63]. We found no disclosure of a pledge over the controlling stake in the annual report; that is an absence of disclosure, not confirmation that the block is unencumbered, and it should be verified with the company before any position is sized.

The board disclosed for the year to 31 December 2025 has three commissioners — Aldi Imam Wibowo as president commissioner, Billy Sabarto, and Yudi Arif as the independent commissioner — and a president director, Imam Subowo Edie [S2 p.32, p.48]. Press in November 2026 attributes the president-director role to Ari Wijayanto, which suggests a change during 2026 that we have not seen in a filing [S4]. The audit committee and the nomination and remuneration functions sit under the board, but with a single independent commissioner out of three, the board's ability to check the controller is limited [S2 p.32]. For a company whose economics depend on a government allocation, that is a material weakness.

Related-party dealings run through the balance sheet rather than the P&L. In June 2024 the company acquired three distributors in transactions the annual report classifies as material and affiliated; the previous shareholders of those entities are disclosed as related parties, and the list includes the president commissioner [S2 p.124, p.306]. The group was also the working-capital lender: trade payables to related parties were IDR378.6bn at end-2024 and IDR4.7bn at end-2025, and long-term other payables to related parties were IDR194.8bn at end-2025 [S2 p.259]. The sales side is clean by comparison — related-party trade receivables are negligible — so the related-party exposure is financing and acquisition, not revenue inflation. That distinction matters: it is an optics-and-structure flag, not a fabrication flag.

The auditor disclosure does not reconcile, and we report it that way rather than as a clean change of firm. The FY2025 shareholders' resolution names KAP Independen Drs Kartoyo dan Rekan as the firm that audited the FY2025 statements [S2 p.136-137], while the governance table lists Heliantono dan Rekan for FY2025, Urda Zismawan for FY2024 and Irfan Zulmendra for FY2023 [S2 p.180]. We found no qualification in the archived text and no explanation of the rotation of names. An unclear audit trail in a year of collapsing cash flow is a governance flag, not proof of anything worse, but a reader should not treat the name on the front of the report as settled. The company paid no dividend for FY2025 [S2 p.115], and its capital return has taken the form of a buyback of up to IDR100.0bn at a maximum price of Rp300 per share, held as treasury and not cancelled [S3]. Buying back shares while net debt rises and free cash flow is negative is a capital-allocation choice we do not endorse; the fact that the ceiling is below the market price makes it largely notional, but the authorisation still signals how the controller thinks about value.

On ESG, the material issues are governance and animal-protein operations rather than emissions disclosure. The company holds halal and food-safety certifications and operates an abattoir and feedlot, so animal welfare, effluent and cold-chain energy are the operating exposures [S2 p.21, p.62]. The annual report describes using feedlot waste as organic fertiliser, which is a small circular initiative rather than a strategy [S7]. The dominant ESG risk is the G: a controller with 70.6% of the shares, affiliate acquisitions, related-party financing and a thin free float 11.7% [S0, S2]. We would need a board with genuine independence and a related-party committee with teeth before we treated the governance discount as closed.

The dated catalysts are the quarterly reporting cycle and the policy cycle. The Q3 2026 financial report is the first test of whether the second-quarter profit collapse was a one-off; our base case assumes the second half does not recover to the prior year's run-rate [S0]. The government's 2027 beef import allocation, expected around the turn of the year, is the single most important event for the investment case [S5]. The FY2026 results in the first quarter should give the first full-year disclosure of the dairy segment and the capex actually spent [S4]. The annual general meeting in the first half will settle the dividend, the related-party balances and the dairy budget [S2]. The buyback window closes in May 2027, and the treatment of the treasury shares will show whether the programme was ever more than a signal [S3].

Between those dates we monitor a short list of KPIs. On the P&L: revenue growth against the FY2026E base of IDR4,752.1bn, gross margin against 6.3%, and the interest line against IDR115.7bn. On the cash flow: operating cash flow, the inventory balance (IDR907.6bn at the last year-end) and trade receivables (IDR217.8bn) — the three items that turned net profit into negative operating cash flow [S2]. On the balance sheet: net debt (IDR1,388.1bn in our base case), the net-debt-to-EBITDA ratio (7.5x) and the rollover of short-term bank lines [S0]. On strategy: the dairy herd, milk volumes, the UHT timeline and the capex bill [S4]; the 2027 quota and permit utilisation [S5]; and any new related-party receivable, guarantee or affiliate transaction [S2]. A quarter that shows positive operating cash flow and a stable gross margin would force us to revisit the SELL; a quota allocation that excludes private processors would confirm the bear case.

bear.narrative: The free-meal programme procurement goes to larger, lower-cost protein suppliers; the private import allocation is cut again in 2027; revenue keeps falling at the H1 2026 rate and the gross margin gives way as competitors bid for the same cattle. The Rp1.4trn of short-term bank lines is refinanced 200bp wider because net debt reaches eight times EBITDA, which is the credit event the prose bear describes; a discounted rights issue is the alternative and would transfer value from existing holders to the new money rather than add to it.

bull.narrative: BEEF wins a visible share of the free-meal programme through its cold-storage network and its dairy herd; the 2027 private allocation is restored toward the 2025 level; the Subang warehouse lifts throughput without new capex and the 6% trading margin holds.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E -26.6% is the filed run-rate, not a forecast step. H1 2026 revenue from the data pack's quarterly series is Rp2,376.0bn (Q1 Rp1,270.5bn + Q2 Rp1,105.5bn) against Rp3,453.6bn in H1 2025; annualising the half at its own rate, rather than assuming a second-half recovery with no order book to support it, gives Rp4,752bn for the year, -26.6% on FY2025 [S0]. Q2 2026 was +2% on Q2 2025, so the decline is the absence of the Q1 2025 import spike rather than a collapsing customer base. FY2027E is held at the filed run-rate, not a recovery: the latest quarter grew 2% year on year, and nothing in the archive supports more. The private-sector import allocation was cut to 30,000 t from 180,000 t for 2026 on two independent association estimates and the 2027 allocation has not been published, the free-meal programme is not named in any BEEF filing, and the dairy has no disclosed volume or start date [S5, S9, S0]. Growth therefore steps from the filed 2% to the long-run 4% nominal GDP rate rather than spiking and fading; a 6% gross-margin distributor does not compound faster than the protein market it serves, and a recovery year would be an assumption with no source behind it.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: FY2025A 6.35% (gross profit Rp410.9bn on Rp6,474.3bn of sales) and FY2024A 6.30%, so the margin is stable at the last actual [S2 p.261]. The input is the margin at the FY2025A deck input prices; the two cost links then charge the reviewed house agri deck's own path at the 80% pass-through set below, so FY2026E reproduces the audited margin rather than drifting below it: corn rises from US$172.6/t in FY2025A to US$214.6/t in FY2026E and soymeal from US$321.2/t to US$411.0/t on the reviewed deck [deck.agri.corn, deck.agri.soymeal], which on 6% of COGS corn-linked and 2% soymeal-linked with a fifth unpassed is 0.06 x 0.243 x 0.20 + 0.02 x 0.279 x 0.20 = 0.40pp of COGS, about 0.38pp of revenue; the constant-price input is therefore 6.72% so that FY2026E lands on 6.35%. We do not hold 6.72% as a forecast margin: it is the FY2025A-anchored level carried through the deck's cost path. The filed H1 2026 gross margin is higher (gross profit Rp188.6bn on Rp2,376.0bn of sales, 7.9%), but H1 opex ran at 4.45% of sales against 2.94% in FY2025, so H1 EBIT margin was 3.5% against the FY2025A 3.43% and the model's 3.35% in FY2026E: the two most recent quarters do not show a margin step-change at the EBIT line, which is the line the valuation uses [S0]. Food Processing is 0.2% of revenue, so there is no brand premium to protect [S2 p.15].

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Corn is about 60% of Indonesian cattle feed; feed is about a quarter of live-cattle cost and domestic cattle about 40% of COGS, so corn-linked cost is roughly 6% of COGS [S2 p.41, S5]. The rest of COGS is imported beef and live cattle priced off world markets and the rupiah, which no deck in the agri complex prices.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: 80%, not a haircut. Beef is sold inside a government reference-price band and the band was revised up as feed and import costs rose: by early 2026 fresh beef was trading at the top of the band and buffalo meat above its reference price [S5]. A 6% gross margin has no room to absorb a permanent feed-cost level shift, so most of it is passed on with a lag; the 20% unpassed is the lag, not a standing squeeze. The H1 2026 filed result confirms the mechanism: net profit of Rp22.3bn implies a gross margin near 6.1%, in line with the FY2025 actual and well above the 5.4% the old 50% pass-through produced [S0].

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Soymeal is about 20% of cattle feed, i.e. roughly 2% of COGS on the same chain: 40% domestic cattle x 25% feed x 20% soymeal [S2 p.41, S5].

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Same 80% pass-through as corn, for the same reason: the reference-price band moves with feed and import costs, and the unpassed fifth is the lag between a cost move and the band revision [S0, S5].

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025A 2.94% (selling Rp66.4bn + G&A Rp123.8bn on Rp6,474.3bn of sales), FY2024A 2.96% [S2 p.261]. Held at 3.0%: the cold-storage network is built, so distribution cost grows with volume rather than ahead of it.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: 0.55%, against FY2025A 0.50% (Rp32.1bn) and FY2024A 0.43% (Rp21.3bn) [S0]. Slightly higher forward because the Subang cold storage (Rp28,000t) came into service in November 2025 and depreciates from a full year in 2026 [S2 p.23].

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025A was 7.8% of revenue (Rp507.0bn) because Subang was under construction; the warehouse was commissioned in November 2025 [S2 p.23]. We step down to 5.0% in FY2026E for the dairy farm and the 30ha Sukabumi land, then 3.5%, 2.5%, 2.0% and 1.5%. The 1.5% terminal rate is set by the balance sheet, not by caution: net PP&E is 14.4% of revenue, so growing it at the 5% revenue rate needs about 0.7% of revenue plus the 0.55% depreciation charge, i.e. roughly 1.2-1.5%. Holding capex at the 3% a distributor "should" spend would make PP&E compound faster than sales forever, which no buyer would underwrite [S2 p.258].

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025A 18.8% (Rp1,214.3bn on Rp6,474.3bn): inventory Rp907.6bn, receivables Rp217.8bn and almost no payables after related-party credit was withdrawn [S2 p.258-259]. The June 2026 balance shows Rp1,070.6bn of operating working capital on annualised H1 revenue of Rp4,752bn, i.e. 22.5%; that annualisation overstates the ratio, because the balance is inflated by the import stock bought for the first-half sales season against a half-year revenue base [S0]. We therefore hold the FY2025-revenue ratio, 18.5%, into FY2026E and 18% thereafter, and disclose that the 21-22% reading is the annualisation, not the company's normal working-capital intensity.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: FY2025A 19.8% (deferred tax of Rp31.8bn, no current tax) and FY2024A 28.1% [S2 p.261]. We use the 22% statutory rate: cash tax should normalise as the deferred-tax asset that flattered 2025 runs out.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: 7.4%, the filed 2026 run-rate, not the 6.5% carried in the first draft. H1 2026 interest of Rp29.35bn in Q1 plus Rp26.04bn in Q2 is Rp55.40bn on average debt of Rp1,495.7bn (opening Rp1,564.1bn, closing Rp1,427.4bn), i.e. 3.70% for the half, 7.4% annualised [S0]. FY2024's own outturn was 8.4% (Rp32.9bn on Rp391bn) and FY2025's 5.1% (Rp59.8bn of net other expense on Rp1,172bn) was a part-year average through a step-up in borrowing, so the filed half-year is the best measure of the current facility mix [S2 p.261, S0]. The engine charges the rate on opening debt, and the FY2025 year-end balance of Rp1,564.1bn is above the H1 average, so this convention charges slightly more interest in FY2026E than the H1 run-rate; the alternative, carrying 6.5% with no filed support, understated FY2026E interest by 8%.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: 1.0% on a tiny average cash balance (Rp18.5bn at end-2025) [S2 p.107].

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: The funding plug, not a forecast of appetite: each year's net borrowing is set equal to the cash-flow deficit before financing (net profit plus D&A less capex less the working-capital move), so cash is held at about the Rp19bn the June 2026 balance reports and every gap is carried as interest-bearing bank debt rather than as negative cash that pays no interest [S0, S2 p.259]. The series is therefore not an assumption about management's appetite: it is the deficit the operating and capex plan creates at the cost of debt set above, and it is re-derived year by year so the model carries no cash earning 1% while borrowing at 7.4%. FY2026E is a repayment because the revenue decline releases working capital; from FY2027E the working-capital rebuild plus capex above depreciation requires new bank lines every year. The Rp1.6trn BMRI/BCA facility signed in October 2025 is the source of that funding capacity [S2 p.259, S5].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Zero: FX and other income are not forecastable and were -Rp59.8bn in FY2025, mostly interest already captured in cost of debt [S2 p.261].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: 0.2% of net profit in FY2025; immaterial minority balances [S0, S2].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Zero in every year. The company has never paid a dividend, has negative operating cash flow and Rp1.5trn of net debt; it authorised a Rp100bn buyback in May 2026 instead [S2, S3].

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Zero. The May 2026 buyback authorises up to Rp100bn for up to 333m shares at a maximum price; the archived authorisation reports no realised volume, and we found no later filing carrying one, so the programme is assumed to be held as treasury and not cancelled and the share count is unchanged [S3].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 4.0%, half of the roughly 8.6% nominal GDP growth the house macro deck carries (real 5.29% plus CPI 3.28%). The discount is not a view that the import regime is being liberalised — it is the opposite: the private-sector import allocation was cut to 30,000 t from 180,000 t in 2026, and the quota regime is a policy choice that can tighten further [S5, S9]. A distributor whose raw material is a rationed licence, whose selling price sits inside an administered band, and whose return on capital is below its cost of capital cannot reinvest at the nominal GDP rate; 4% prices real volume growth in the protein market net of the share the state traders are taking.

challenges.challenge: The engine returns Rp93.24 for base, bear and bull alike (fund record valuation.scenarios; packet base 50pc to 93, bear 25pc to 93, bull 25pc to 93). The declared minus 3pp growth and minus 1pp margin shocks never reach the target because the DCF is floored at zero and both multiples read FY2025A lines. The probability-weighted target and the -74.9pc expected return are single-path base-case outputs.
challenges.answer: The 93 target is withdrawn. The published target is labelled the base case and we no longer publish a probability-weighted target or weighted language: the engine multiple legs read trailing market data and the DCF floors at zero in base and bear, so a weighted average would be the base case dressed as a distribution. Sections 4 and 5 say this explicitly and report the shocked forecast paths [S0].

challenges.challenge: The quota cut carries the thesis, but its only source (S5) is internally impossible: 30,000t national quota, 17,000t to private processors and 100,000t to two BUMN. The report notes this cannot reconcile yet still states cut to 30,000t from 180,000t as fact. No primary regulation is cited and BEEF's own 2026 allocation is absent; the annual report's only quota disclosure is 2018-20 (12,000 head and 2,458,260kg, S2 p.63).
challenges.answer: The quota arithmetic is corrected from a second source: 30,000 t is the private-sector allocation, not the national quota, and the national quota is 297,000 t, so the figures reconcile. APPDI (S9) and Nampa (S5) agree on 30,000 t from 180,000 t. The quota is restated as association evidence, not a primary schedule, and BEEF's own 2026 tonnage is disclosed as absent [S9][S5].
